questions.question_text: A survey question asks: 'Considering that public libraries provide vital community services, should council increase library funding?' Which type of bias is present in this question?

options.text: Leading question
Double-barrelled question
options.why: A double-barrelled question asks two separate questions in one stem, whereas this question asks only about library funding.

options.text: Overlapping categories
options.why: Overlapping categories refers to numerical response bins that share endpoints, not question stems.

options.text: Assumed-fact question
options.why: An assumed-fact question presupposes an unverified personal condition, such as owning a car or smoking.

questions.solution_text:
The question includes one-sided praise ('vital community services') to persuade the respondent to support funding.
Leading question.

questions.question_text: A draft survey item reads: 'How bad was the traffic congestion during your morning commute?' Which rewrite best removes bias while offering a balanced set of choices?

options.text: 'How would you rate the traffic flow during your commute: Heavy, Moderate, or Light?'
'Don't you agree that morning traffic is unacceptable: Yes or No?'
options.why: This replacement is still leading and uses biased phrasing.

options.text: 'How terrible was the traffic congestion: Extremely bad or Very bad?'
options.why: This replacement uses emotive language and offers only negative choices.

options.text: 'Why is the morning traffic so slow?'
options.why: This replacement assumes traffic is slow and provides no structured response choices.

questions.solution_text:
The original question uses the negative word 'bad'. The neutral rewrite uses objective phrasing with balanced choices from Heavy to Light.
'How would you rate the traffic flow during your commute: Heavy, Moderate, or Light?'

questions.question_text:
A market research firm surveys teenagers about their mental health history.
Which practice is an essential ethical requirement for this study?

options.text: Obtaining informed consent from participants (and guardians) and guaranteeing confidentiality
Requiring participants to provide their home address to verify eligibility
options.why: Collecting home addresses increases privacy risks and is unnecessary for demographic validity.

options.text: Making survey completion compulsory for all selected students
options.why: Ethical research requires voluntary participation, never forced completion.

options.text: Publishing individual responses publicly to ensure research transparency
options.why: Publicly releasing individual sensitive data is a severe breach of privacy.

questions.solution_text:
Ethical research involving minors and sensitive health topics requires informed consent and strict data confidentiality.
Obtaining informed consent from participants (and guardians) and guaranteeing confidentiality.

questions.question_text:
A nationwide census form asks respondents to select their marital status from the options: 'Married' and 'Single'.
Why does this question violate questionnaire design and diversity standards?

options.text: The options are not exhaustive and omit relationships such as de facto, divorced, or widowed
The question is double-barrelled
options.why: The question asks about a single attribute (marital status), not two separate topics.

options.text: The question uses leading and emotive language
options.why: The words 'Married' and 'Single' are neutral descriptive terms, not emotive language.

options.text: The options contain overlapping categories
options.why: Married and Single are mutually exclusive, so they do not overlap; the fault is incompleteness.

questions.solution_text:
The provided options leave out common legal and social statuses, forcing respondents into inaccurate categories.
The options are not exhaustive and omit relationships such as de facto, divorced, or widowed.

questions.question_text: A survey asks: 'Do you support improving public transport and building more toll roads?' Which fault makes this question unreliable?

options.text: It is a double-barrelled question that combines two distinct policies into one answer
It contains overlapping response categories
options.why: Overlapping categories refers to option ranges sharing boundaries, not stem issues.

options.text: It assumes the respondent owns a vehicle
options.why: The stem does not presuppose vehicle ownership, it asks about broad infrastructure policies.

options.text: It breaches respondent anonymity
options.why: The question content itself does not collect or reveal personal identifying data.

questions.solution_text:
A respondent may support public transport but oppose toll roads. Combining them prevents a clear single response.
It is a double-barrelled question that combines two distinct policies into one answer.

questions.question_text: A workplace questionnaire asks: 'How often do you smoke cigarettes during work breaks?' Which issue is present in this question?

options.text: It is an assumed-fact question that presumes the employee is a smoker
It contains double-barrelled wording
options.why: The question asks about one single behaviour (smoking frequency), not two.

options.text: It violates accessibility by using complex technical jargon
options.why: The question uses simple everyday English, not technical jargon.

options.text: It uses emotive adjectives to manipulate opinions
options.why: The question contains no emotive adjectives, but rather presupposes a fact.

questions.solution_text:
The question presupposes that every respondent smokes cigarettes, leaving non-smokers without a proper response path.
It is an assumed-fact question that presumes the employee is a smoker.

questions.question_text:
An employer conducts an anonymous employee satisfaction survey.
The survey system secretly records the IP address and exact submission timestamp of each employee, enabling managers to identify individual respondents.
Why is this an ethical breach?

options.text: It violates participant privacy and breaches the guarantee of anonymity
It makes the survey questions leading and emotive
options.why: Secretly recording IP addresses is a data ethics violation, not a question wording issue.

options.text: It creates overlapping response categories in the questions
options.why: IP tracking affects privacy, not the mathematical categories of response options.

options.text: It forces the survey to become double-barrelled
options.why: Double-barrelled questions relate to combining topics in question stems, not tracking data.

questions.solution_text:
Promising anonymity while secretly gathering identifying metadata violates informed consent and respondent privacy.
It violates participant privacy and breaches the guarantee of anonymity.

questions.question_text:
A community sports organisation collects feedback from local families.
The survey is distributed exclusively via a smartphone app that requires facial scanning and is available only in English.
What modification best improves cultural responsiveness and accessibility?

options.text: Provide translated paper and web versions with standard anonymous login options
Double the number of leading questions in the survey
options.why: Leading questions increase bias rather than improving cultural accessibility.

options.text: Require all participants to complete the survey in under two minutes
options.why: Time limits hinder accessibility for people with reading or language difficulties.

options.text: Remove all response options other than 'Agree' and 'Disagree'
options.why: Restricting response options reduces data quality and does not resolve accessibility.

questions.solution_text:
Offering multiple languages, non-intrusive login, and accessible physical formats ensures broad community participation.
Provide translated paper and web versions with standard anonymous login options.
